A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RoboData and multimodal manipulation framework, renamed from RoboMM to RoboTron-Mani. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoboMM benchmark evaluations, component and alignment ablations, and an OpenVLA comparison in Tables 1–3, with task-level results in the appendix.

after.justification: V2 reports original RoboTron-Mani evaluations, additional ablations, RT-1/SIMPLER results, and a ten-task physical-robot experiment, alongside retained earlier results.

M1.justification: V1 uses an MLP action decoder. V2 Section 2.2 and Figure 4 introduce a CogACT-style DiT alternative, which is used for the main joint-training results and explicitly compared with the MLP in Table 2. This changes a central action-generation component; UVFormer, MIM, and the auxiliary decoders remain.

E1.justification: V1 evaluates five simulation datasets. V2 retains CALVIN, Meta-World, LIBERO, and RoboCasa, adds RT-1 training data with SIMPLER evaluation on three task families, and adds ten physical UR3 manipulation tasks. RoboMimic results disappear, although its dataset documentation remains.

E2.justification: V2 adds jointly trained RoboFlamingo comparisons across four simulation datasets, π0 and π-Fast on LIBERO, DTP on CALVIN, and GR00T-N1-2B+IDM on RoboCasa. New RT-1 comparisons include RT-X, Octo, OpenVLA, and HPT; physical experiments compare RoboUniView and RoboFlamingo. The IBC comparison disappears with RoboMimic, while the original CALVIN/OpenVLA comparison survives in appendix Table 6.

E3.justification: The main joint-training configuration now uses the DiT head, and the alignment study is described as four-dataset training. New RT-1 experiments introduce camera-parameter supplementation and missing-wrist-image masking. Physical evaluation uses 100 demonstrations per task and ten trials per task with manual resets. The original single-frame OpenVLA protocol is retained in the appendix.

E4.justification: The existing ablation program gains an Image-plus-UVFormer configuration without occupancy supervision and an explicit MLP-versus-DiT comparison in Table 2. Table 3 extends the retained alignment analysis with aligned and unaligned RoboFlamingo controls. The RoboMimic alignment results are omitted; the other original proposed-model alignment scores remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report point success rates and average sequence lengths without independent training-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The new physical trial counts specify evaluation sample sizes rather than a new uncertainty-reporting practice.

E6.justification: V2 reports substantially different benchmark and task-level results under its revised configuration: RoboCasa is 47.4% in Table 1 versus 30.6% in v1, with the older score retained in alignment Table 3. Table 2 retains the 3.31 MLP result and adds 3.51 for DiT. New results include 60.0% on RT-1 and 82.5%, 70.0%, and 46.6% across physical-task difficulty groups. These are not same-setting version-to-version gains.

T1.justification: The mathematical content of Equations 1–14, the losses, coordinate transformations, and EADM/CRMM/PCM definitions is retained. The DiT addition introduces no new formal derivation, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: V2 strengthens the abstract and introduction from a competitive generalist policy to the first generalist policy surpassing expert models, and explicitly claims state-of-the-art results on simulated and real-world datasets. The headline CALVIN sequence-length claim changes from 1.7–3.3 to 1.7–3.5, expanding the claimed achievement and applicability.

C2.justification: V2 extends the alignment explanation by arguing that camera changes alter 2D features while preserving 3D scene features, and interprets RoboFlamingo's results as showing an inability to align input space. It also attributes physical-task advantages to stronger 3D reasoning. The existing moderate-training-scale qualification and interpretation of imperfect auxiliary predictions remain.

D1.justification: V2 adds substantial physical-system documentation: UR3/Dalu hardware, gripper and camera models, hand-eye calibration, point-cloud supervision, ROS1, and RTX 3090 operation. It newly specifies a four-billion-parameter bf16 model and RT-1 preprocessing. Reported joint-training time changes from 130 to about 50 hours under the revised experiment, and the repository pointer changes. Existing appendix hyperparameters remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds references to CogACT, π0, FAST, GR00T N1, and DTP, while removing MindBench and IBC. It adds an RT-1-X versus RT-1 argument about heterogeneous-data fusion. The dedicated related-work discussion otherwise remains largely unchanged after relocation.

P1.justification: The main narrative is substantially reorganized: Related Work and the OpenVLA comparison move to the appendix, alignment receives a separate experimental subsection, and the conclusion is rewritten as Conclusion and Outlook. The abstract and results discussion are revised, alongside the model renaming and author-header changes. Much of the technical exposition is retained.

P2.justification: V2 redraws the overview chart, revises architecture diagrams to display the DiT alternative, adds the physical-task montage, and updates the rollout montage. Benchmark Table 1 is reorganized, Table 2 gains configurations, and alignment results receive a separate display. New physical and RT-1 tables substantially expand the presentation; the unchanged OpenVLA table moves to the appendix.

improvement.justification: V2 addresses important gaps in v1's simulation-only validation and limited generalist comparisons through the ten-task physical study, jointly trained RoboFlamingo controls, and additional action-head and alignment ablations. These substantially strengthen practical validation and support for the design choices. Lost RoboMimic results, absent uncertainty estimates, and stale documentation such as Figure 9's RoboMimic caption remain weaknesses. The improvement rests on stronger empirical support, rather than treating scores from changed configurations as controlled performance gains.
